deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. The page determines the coefficient of terrestrial refraction from reciprocal, simultaneous zenith distances measured at pairs of stations in Gauss's 1824 Hanoverian triangulation. The stations are Wilsede, Steinberg, Brüttendorf, Zeven, Bottel, Elmhorst, Litberg, Bremen, Brelit, Garlste, Bullerberg, Falkenberg and Hamburg. The previous page derived height differences from the same data.

COLUMNS. For each line between stations P and P' the table gives:
(1) C = the curvature, i.e. the angle at the Earth's centre subtended by the line, in arcseconds. The header is hard to read; the later phrase 'Summe der ersten 22 Krümmungen' identifies it.
(2) z + z' - 180°, the sum of the two observed zenith distances minus 180°, in arcseconds.
(3) R = (1) - (2). Geometry gives z + z' = 180° + C - (ρ + ρ'), where ρ and ρ' are the refractions at the two ends. So R = ρ + ρ' is the total refraction.
(4) μ = R/C, the refraction ratio for that line. This is the modern coefficient k = r_earth/r_ray, since ρ ≈ kC/2 at each end.
Example: 1564.883 - 1281.286 = 283.597, and 283.597/1564.883 = 0.18123.

GROUPING. 25 lines are listed. The first 22 lie above a rule. The last three (Wilsede–Bullerberg, Litberg–Hamburg, Bottel–Steinberg) lie below it and are kept separate.

SUMMARY RESULTS (right-hand side).
- Sum of the first 22 curvatures: ΣC = 22549.844".
- Sum of the corresponding refractions: ΣR = 3332.329".
- Ratio ΣR/ΣC = 0.14778. This is the least-squares estimate of μ for the model R_i = μ·C_i with weights 1/C_i, i.e. a 'ratio of sums' estimator.
- Unweighted mean of the 22 individual ratios: 0.14499.
- Mean error of one refraction: 30.07". Exact recipe not shown. My reconstruction (mine): residuals R_i - 0.14778·C_i over all 25 lines, sum of squares ≈ 21570, divided by n - 1 = 24 gives about 30.0", close to 30.07". Using only the 22 lines gives about 31.5" (n - 1) or 30.8" (n).
- 'Also mittlerer Fehler einer relativen Höhe r/13720'. Arithmetic: half of 30.07" is 15.035", and 15.035"/206264.8" = 1/13719. So r/13720 is the height error produced by a 15" angular error over distance r. Here r is most plausibly the length of the line, not the Earth radius. This is the error of a height difference attributable to one end's refraction, taking half the total-refraction error.

MARGINAL NOTE (pencil). It records that the result was contained in a letter to Schumacher, apparently dated 28 November 1824.
errors: Zeven–Steinberg: 236.615/1080.225 = 0.219042, but the page gives 0.21908 (a slip of about 4e-5, unless the last digit is misread). The mean 0.14499 was computed with 0.21908 as written; with 0.21904 it would be 0.144988, which still rounds to 0.14499.
Brüttendorf–Bottel: 103.408/815.727 = 0.126767, written 0.12676 (truncated rather than rounded; negligible).

The derivation of the mean error 30.07" is not shown. My recomputation gives about 29.98" (25 lines, n - 1) or 31.5" (22 lines, n - 1), so the exact procedure cannot be confirmed. This is not necessarily an error.
All 25 differences in column 3 check exactly. Both column sums (22549.844 and 3332.329), the ratio 0.14778 and the mean 0.14499 are correct.

results.what: Coefficient of terrestrial refraction from reciprocal simultaneous zenith distances: k = (C - (z + z' - 180°))/C, with the overall value ΣR/ΣC = 0.1478 from 22 lines and an unweighted mean of 0.1450.
results.modern_name: Coefficient of refraction k (ratio of Earth radius to ray radius), determined by reciprocal trigonometric levelling
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (k ≈ 0.13 from the Hanoverian survey) and Bessel; the reciprocal-zenith-distance method goes back to the 18th century (Delambre, Lambert and others).

results.what: Weighted (ratio-of-sums) estimator compared with the mean of the individual ratios, plus a mean error of one refraction (30.07").
results.modern_name: Least-squares estimate of a proportionality constant; standard error of a single observation

results.what: Propagation of the refraction uncertainty into the error of a relative height: σ_h = r × (15.03" in radians) = r/13720.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine data reduction from Gauss's own Hanoverian survey. His determination of the refraction coefficient (about 0.13) is well known, and the 1824 value was communicated to Schumacher. The page is a working record of that, with nothing methodologically new.

checkable.asserts: Total refraction for Wilsede–Steinberg equals curvature minus (z + z' - 180°); result 0.
μ for Zeven–Steinberg = 0.219042, not 0.21908 as written.
Half of 30.07" in radians is 1/13719, matching r/13720.

transcription_corrections: The column header over the first column is uncertain. The machine reading 'Drehung [?] des Erdbogens [?]' is doubtful; the content is the curvature (Krümmung), i.e. the central angle in arcseconds.
The 'μ' header sits above the ratio column (column 4), not above the refraction column.
A horizontal rule separates the first 22 lines from the last three (Wilsede–Bullerberg, Litberg–Hamburg, Bottel–Steinberg); only the first 22 enter the sums.
Pencil note: read roughly as 'enthalten in dem Briefe an Schumacher, 28 November 1824' (partly illegible).
Zeven–Steinberg ratio is written 0,21908; the arithmetically correct value is 0.21904.
